articles.title: ‘It’s hard to sell a house when it’s covered in baboon faeces’: Cape Town divided over plan to remove its monkeys
articles.summary:
Two troops of chacma baboons are breaking into homes and shops but animal rights activists insist coexistence is the answer

Cape Town’s city council has said it will “imminently” round up two baboon troops coming into repeated conflict with residents. The animals will be sterilised and permanently moved to a newly constructed sanctuary. The plan has been fiercely criticised by animal rights activists, who say the monkeys should remain roaming freely, and that less destructive options have not been properly considered.

Cape Town’s baboon problem has been brewing since the 2000s, after the city stopped culling troops in the late 1990s after pressure from the public. But in the past two years it has reached boiling point. A 2025 census found that the population had grown by a third since 2000, from 360 baboons to 493, now living in 12 managed troops.

articles.title: Children forced to give up school for work as fighting upends daily life in Yemen
articles.summary:
Renewed fighting between Iran-aligned Houthis and Saudi-backed Yemeni forces has shattered four years of relative calm

In the mornings, 13-year-old Muneer Farie went to school, and in the afternoons he helped his father feed the livestock. He took his studies seriously, dreaming of becoming the first teacher in his family of farmers.

As fighting approached his village in al-Wazeyah district in Taiz, Yemen, two weeks ago, Muneer’s focus started to drift from his lessons. The classroom echoed with the distant sounds of explosions and gunfire. His home was suddenly on the frontline of renewed fighting between the Iran-aligned Houthis and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government.

articles.title: Turkey’s $17bn fund scandal becomes a political crisis for Erdogan
articles.summary:
Turkey’s $17bn fund scandal becomes a political crisis for Erdogan

Submitted by Ragip Soylu on Tue, 09/29/2026 - 10:22
President vows accountability as the liquidation of 130 investment funds exposes ties to Turkey’s ruling elite
A picture taken in Istanbul shows US dollar banknotes and Turkish lira banknotes, 27 January 2021 (Ozan Kose/AFP)
Off

A crisis involving Turkish investment funds accused of running Ponzi-like schemes has affected half a million people, with authorities ordering the liquidation of some 130 funds worth $17bn earlier this month.

Already historic in scale, the financial turmoil has quickly become a major political crisis for President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s administration, exposing a web of connections between the funds, their managers and the ruling elite.

The most prominent political casualty so far has been Fatma Betul Sayan Kaya, a deputy head of the ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP) and family minister from 2016 to 2018. She resigned on Sunday after the opposition accused her of making substantial profits from share sales shortly before the funds crisis triggered a major stock market sell-off on 16 September.

Erdogan addressed the controversy on Monday, pledging to pursue those responsible for market manipulation and fraudulent trading schemes.

“Whoever lays a hand on the nation's rights, assets or legal interests will face us and the state,” he said.

The funds in question concentrated their holdings in illiquid stocks with low free floats, making their prices easier to inflate because relatively few shares were available for trading. For example, the Tera investment fund generated a return of over 1,500 percent over the past year, a figure that is totally illogical by any market calculation or method.

Authorities have set a six-month timeline to sell the funds’ assets and repay investors. But experts are pessimistic about how much investors will recover, with many unlikely to receive the inflated gains reflected in their holdings. Many of those affected are believed to be ruling-party voters, potentially increasing the political cost.

Brokerage firms and financial groups accused of involvement in the alleged schemes, including Tera Group and Pusula, have politically connected figures on their boards. Tera and others deny wrongdoing.

One of Erdogan’s chief advisers served on the board of Tera Portfolio Management until January 2026. Another former presidential adviser remained on the board until the crisis erupted, while his brother, a former ambassador, also sat on the boards of several companies under Tera Holding.

'Whoever lays a hand on the nation's rights, assets, or legal interests will face us and the state'

- President Erdogan

Tera Group chairman Emre Tezmen, who has been arrested on charges of running a Ponzi-like scheme, also held a senior position in Turkey’s capital markets infrastructure. He served on the board of the Central Securities Depository of Turkey (MKK) until his arrest, the official institution responsible for the electronic recording, safekeeping and transfer of securities and other financial instruments. Tezmen denies wrongdoing.

Muhammed Yariz, the chairman of Pusula Portfolio, has also recently been arrested. He is known for his past work within the AKP.

The connections extend beyond the investment firms themselves.

Kaya’s disputed trades primarily involved shares in Ozata Denizcilik, a shipbuilder involved in projects for the Turkish navy. The company’s links to politically connected families have raised questions about the overlap between businesses, regulators and government officials.

An Ozata Denizcilik board member arrested on Monday is the son of a former member of the banking regulator that approved Tera Investment Bank, a sister company of Tera’s brokerage business.

At one point, Tera’s brokerage reportedly controlled 95 percent of Ozata Denizcilik’s shares. The shipbuilder’s valuation surged to $5bn, exceeding those of major Turkish companies such as automaker Ford Otosan and steel producer Eregli.

The arrested board member is also the son-in-law of a deputy finance minister, linking him to the very ministry now tasked with helping resolve the crisis.

In a statement on social media, the board member denied the charges, stating that he surrendered to the authorities voluntarily in order to clear his name. 

It remains unclear how far accountability will extend. Rumours circulating in Ankara suggest that other senior officials may have been involved, either by turning a blind eye to questionable activities or by investing themselves. Those claims remain unverified.

High 'political cost' expected

The authorities’ response has also been marked by missteps.

On Friday, Justice Minister Akin Gurlek announced that authorities had frozen the assets of 46 legal entities, 18 funds and 42 individuals after reviewing fund outflows between 1 July and 16 September. Travel bans were also imposed on 37 suspects as a judicial-control measure.

The measures blocked asset transfers, sales, large cash withdrawals and other transactions that could reduce the assets available for recovery. They also required capital market instruments to be frozen and suspicious transactions to be reported to judicial authorities.

Turkey busts Israel-linked 'scam empire' behind alleged $266m fraud
Read More »

The affected entities spanned investment firms, financial services companies, insurers, food producers and other businesses. They included Tera Yatirim, Pusula Yatirim, Ulusoy Un, Tatilbudur, Enuygun, Astor Enerji, IC Ictas, Emin Evim, Turkiye Hayat ve Emeklilik, Yayla Agro, Turkiye Sigorta and Katilimevim.

The sweeping order raised fears of severe disruption when Borsa Istanbul reopened on Monday, prompting the authorities to reverse it on Sunday.

Astor Enerji, one of the exchange’s largest listed companies, with a market capitalisation of $5.3bn, said on Monday that the restrictions and freezing orders affecting it had been lifted. Its operations were continuing uninterrupted, the company added.

Despite the reversal, the fallout continued, with Turkish stocks falling 2.38 percent on Monday.

Erdogan is due to chair a committee meeting on Tuesday to discuss the next steps, with the mechanism for repaying investors still undecided.

Some analysts in Ankara believe the government may have to sacrifice more politically connected figures, as it has the former family minister, to contain public anger. They argue that the scandal is unlikely to have a major impact on the 2028 presidential election.

Others disagree.

“Erdogan will have to genuinely go after this to show that he doesn’t forgive such transgressions, because the political cost could be worse than people imagine,” an Ankara insider said.

articles.title: UAE confirms Netanyahu visit for first time, with no mention of regional wars
articles.summary:
UAE confirms Netanyahu visit for first time, with no mention of regional wars

Submitted by MEE staff on Tue, 09/29/2026 - 10:38
The visit follows reports that bin Zayed warned Netanyahu of a Hamas operation before 7 October
Emirati President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al-Nahyan in Berlin on 10 September 2026 (Ralf Hirschberger/AFP)
Off

The UAE has officially acknowledged hosting Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for talks with President Mohammed bin Zayed on Sunday, its first such acknowledgement since establishing relations with Israel in 2020.

In a statement late on Monday, the Emirates News Agency said simply that bin Zayed "discussed with the Israeli prime minister the bilateral relations between the two countries and ways to strengthen and develop them".

The UAE released no official photograph of Sunday’s meeting. Its statement made no mention of the regional wars in which the UAE and Israel are involved - in occupied Palestine, Lebanon, Syria, Iran, Yemen and Sudan.

Sources in the UAE told Haaretz that bin Zayed greeted Netanyahu at the airport.

The meeting also made the front pages of the UAE’s state-owned Al-Bayan and Al-Ittihad newspapers, which simply reprinted the official statement.

In May, Netanyahu’s office blindsided the UAE by revealing that he had secretly visited the country at the height of the Israeli-US war on Iran.

The Emirati foreign ministry responded by saying its relations with Israel "are public" and "not based on non-transparent or unofficial arrangements".

"Any claims regarding unannounced visits or undisclosed arrangements are entirely unfounded unless officially announced by the relevant authorities in the UAE," the statement said.

'Moral support'

The latest meeting follows a Haaretz report earlier this month that bin Zayed had given Netanyahu advance warning of a Hamas attack before 7 October 2023.

According to the Israeli newspaper, bin Zayed delivered the warning during a 45-minute phone call about a week and a half before the attack.

UAE president 'told Netanyahu' of Hamas plan for major 'event' ahead of 7 October 2023
Read More »

The revelations come as Netanyahu fights for his political survival ahead of Israel’s upcoming elections.

He also faces corruption charges in Israeli courts and could go to prison if convicted.

During the latest meeting, it was reported that Netanyahu asked bin Zayed to deny its report about the warning and provide “moral” support.

Netanyahu's Office also confirmed the visit, saying he and his wife, Sara, travelled to the UAE on Sunday at the invitation of Mohammed bin Zayed.

"The visit focused on strengthening relations between the two countries and on regional challenges," the official statement read, adding that Netanyahu was accompanied by the head of the National Security Council, the head of the Mossad, the military secretary and the foreign policy adviser.

According to Israeli media reports, representatives from Saudi Arabia, Jordan, Libya, Qatar and Morocco were also present at the meeting.

Ynet reported that Mossad chief Roman Goffman arranged the meeting after Saudi Arabia requested Israeli assistance against Houthi attacks in the Red Sea region.

articles.title: Council of Europe tells Serbia to implement judgement on Bahraini political prisoner
articles.summary:
Council of Europe tells Serbia to implement judgement on Bahraini political prisoner

Submitted by Oscar Rickett on Tue, 09/29/2026 - 07:00
Ahmed Jaafar Mohamed Ali was extradited from Serbia and has been in Bahrain's Jau Prison since 2022
Ahmed Jaafar Mohamed Ali has been held in Jau Prison since he was deported from Serbia in January 2022 (ADHRB)
Off

The Council of Europe has called on Serbia to implement a European Court of Human Rights judgement, which held that the Balkan country had violated the European Convention on Human Rights when it extradited a Bahraini activist seeking asylum. 

Ahmed Jaafar Mohamed Ali travelled to Serbia to seek asylum in November 2021 but was arrested by authorities there based on an Interpol red notice, which Ali’s lawyers say was unlawfully issued. 

The European Court of Human Rights issued an interim measure in January 2022 calling on Serbian authorities to refrain from extraditing Ali pending more information and particularly given the risk of torture or ill-treatment if he was returned. 

Three days later, campaigners say a private plane, chartered by United Arab Emirates-based Royal Jet Airlines, took Ali to Bahrain.

Ever since then the activist, who fled Bahrain in 2011 and then lived in Iran before travelling to Serbia, has been held in Bahrain’s Jau Prison on two life sentences.

Inside the prison, Ali says he has been beaten, denied medical treatment, had his faith insulted and held in solitary confinement. 

According to a recent call with fellow activists, a transcript of which was seen by Middle East Eye, Ali is currently being held in the prison’s Building Two, which houses violent offenders and those on serious drug charges.

Inside the building, the activist says these prisoners - acting on instruction from prison guards - beat and abuse him, creating a climate of fear that never lifts.

European ruling on Serbia 

In March 2025, the European Court of Human Rights ruled that Serbia had violated Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR) by extraditing Ali in defiance of an interim court block.

Article 3 of the convention safeguards against torture and inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment. The Serbian courts violated this when they failed to examine Ali’s complaint that he would face ill-treatment if sent back to Bahrain.

He is stuck in a severely overcrowded cell, has repeatedly had to resort to hunger strikes just to secure basic rights, and has been in and out of solitary confinement

- Sayed Ahmed Alwadaei, Bird

The ECHR ordered Serbia to pay 9,800 euros ($11,100), plus any tax chargeable and interest in the event of a default in payment. 

The Council of Europe’s Committee of Ministers says that, since the judgement, Serbia has placed a sum of money for Ali in a deposit account in a domestic court. 

However, the committee acknowledged his lawyers’ argument that there are “difficulties in complying with the conditions for the release of the funds given the exceptional nature of [Ali’s] situation” in Jau Prison.

The Council of Europe has said that Serbia should “co-operate with [Ali’s] representatives and the Secretariat to find solutions to enable the release of funds to take place without delay”.

Sayed Ahmed Alwadaei, director of advocacy at the Bahrain Institute for Rights and Democracy (Bird), told MEE that he had also been held in Building Two at Jau Prison, and that talking to Ali recently had brought back, in vivid detail, the suffering he had experienced there.   

“It was very hard to hear Ahmed describing to me the degrading conditions he is living in at Jau Prison. He is stuck in a severely overcrowded cell, has repeatedly had to resort to hunger strikes just to secure basic rights, and has been in and out of solitary confinement,” Alwadaei said.
 
“This decision is an important reminder that Serbia cannot simply take Bahrain’s assurances at face value. It must face the reality of what happened after Ahmed’s unlawful extradition and do everything it can to protect him.”

Political prisoners in Bahrain

Last year, Amnesty said that an estimated 322 political prisoners remained arbitrarily detained in Bahrain. 

Bahrain Grand Prix: Twenty years of dissent and sportswashing
Read More »

In the wake of the Arab Spring uprising of 2011, thousands of Bahrainis – mostly from the Sunni-ruled kingdom’s majority Shia population – were arrested and thrown in prison.

In 2024, Bahrain granted 1,500 prisoners royal pardons, and other similar moves have followed, but, according to Amnesty, the government continues to “suppress the rights to freedom of expression, association and peaceful assembly, including through arbitrary detention and prosecutions”. 

The US-Israeli war on Iran has also resulted in a new crackdown from Bahraini authorities, including stripping citizenship from those expressing anything deemed to be supportive of Iran, which has struck targets inside Bahrain.

In his recent call from Jau Prison, Ali described being kept in an overcrowded cell in which half the inmates had to sleep on the floor and in which a lack of ventilation resulted in “suffocating” conditions.

In July, he says he was badly beaten, and he remains “under threat at any moment” from the same “gang”. 

The toilet and washing facilities are unsanitary, he said, with prisoners relying on a hose to wash themselves and overflowing drains.

articles.title: Fighting in Yemen displaces 16,000 over past week: IOM
articles.summary:
Fighting in Yemen displaces 16,000 over past week: IOM

The ongoing fighting in Yemen has displaced nearly 16,000 people the past week, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) said Monday.

The UN agency indicated that 145,308 people (around 24,218 households) were displaced across eight governorates since insecurity escalated on the western coast in June

The total rose by 12 percent, or 15,870 people, between 21 to 28 September. 

"Every week, we count thousands more people who have left everything behind,” said IOM’s chief of mission in Yemen Abdusattor Esoev.

"Behind these figures are parents trying to keep their children safe, older people who cannot travel far, and families who had very little to begin with."

"They need help now, and our response has to move as fast as they are,” he stressed, adding that families are in urgent need of shelter, food and protection.
